Most of the Civil War battles were fought in the South. Historians can use diaries to learn about the condition of the Southern states at the end of the Civil War. The diary entries below come from

, a white Southern teenager who lived in the Confederate city of Columbia, South Carolina. Read modified excerpts of three of her diary entries from around the end of the war. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: Yesterday afternoon we walked all over the town.…I meant last night to write down some description of what I had seen, but was too wretchedly depressed and miserable to even think of it.…It is even worse than I thought. The place is literally in ruins. The entire heart of the city is in ashes—only the outer edges remain.

We were visited yesterday by a squad of Yankees under Lieut. Brett. How the sight of that blue uniform makes my blood boil! The sight fills me with such horrid feelings that I keep in the back parlor and dining room and close the blinds when I go to my bedroom. These men seem to be the meanest type of nation. Their presence has put an end to our pleasant evening re-unions—to our walks—in fact to everything.

pieces.text: We have corn, a little flour and a few vegetables. We have not had any meat until the past few days when mother has bought a little bacon, but I cannot eat bacon. Yesterday we had a little piece of beef—a luxury indeed—the first we have tasted since Sherman passed through. We have no fruit except blackberries and wild plums, although I hear it is a plentiful fruit season. The Yankees are issuing rations but they are only drawn by people in actual need or who have no self-respect.

Most of the Civil War battles were fought in the South. Historians can use diaries to learn about the condition of the Southern states at the end of the Civil War. The diary entries below come from

, a white Southern teenager who lived in the Confederate city of Columbia, South Carolina. Read modified excerpts of three of her diary entries from around the end of the war. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: Yesterday afternoon we walked all over the town.…I meant last night to write down some description of what I had seen, but was too wretchedly depressed and miserable to even think of it.…It is even worse than I thought. The place is literally in ruins. The entire heart of the city is in ashes—only the outer edges remain.

We were visited yesterday by a squad of Yankees under Lieut. Brett. How the sight of that blue uniform makes my blood boil! The sight fills me with such horrid feelings that I keep in the back parlor and dining room and close the blinds when I go to my bedroom. These men seem to be the meanest type of nation. Their presence has put an end to our pleasant evening re-unions—to our walks—in fact to everything.

pieces.text: We have corn, a little flour and a few vegetables. We have not had any meat until the past few days when mother has bought a little bacon, but I cannot eat bacon. Yesterday we had a little piece of beef—a luxury indeed—the first we have tasted since Sherman passed through. We have no fruit except blackberries and wild plums, although I hear it is a plentiful fruit season. The Yankees are issuing rations but they are only drawn by people in actual need or who have no self-respect.

Conflict over the law emerged again almost a year later when President Johnson fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, a supporter of Radical Reconstruction, without Senate approval.

textContent.text: In 1867, Republicans passed a series of laws to protect their Radical Reconstruction plans from interference by President Johnson. One law, the Tenure of Office Act, required Senate approval to remove secretaries from the president's cabinet. President Johnson vetoed it, but Congress quickly overrode the veto to allow the bill to become law. Conflict over the law emerged again almost a year later when President Johnson fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, a supporter of Radical Reconstruction, without Senate approval.

pieces.text: Three days after the firing, House Republicans voted unanimously to approve eleven

The trial lasted nearly two months and ended when the Senate fell one vote short of the number needed to remove Johnson from office. Johnson remained president, but the impeachment process severely damaged his political career.
